content: A leaving group refers to an atom or a group of atoms that detaches from a chemical compound during a reaction. The molecule or fragment that remains after the departure of the leaving group is referred to as the residual or main part of the compound. The term leaving group is context-dependent and varies based on the specific chemical reaction being discussed. The ability of a functional group to leave is termed lability. Leaving groups influence the intrinsic reactivity of a reaction but do not affect nucleophilic discrimination factors. A general rule is that the lower the pKa of the conjugate acid of the leaving group, the better its ability to leave. This is because a lower pKa indicates a more stable conjugate base, which is less likely to react with the cation formed after the leaving group departs. Poor leaving groups, on the other hand, lack this stability and may re-enter the reaction, leading to a cyclic process. This is why strong bases are considered poor leaving groups. In SN1 reactions, halides, pseudohalides, and non-coordinating ions are preferred as leaving groups. Halide salts are particularly effective because they can be abstracted by silver ions to form insoluble silver halides. The sequence of lability in water at room temperature is as follows (from least to most labile): amine (NH2−), methoxy (CH3O−), hydroxyl (HO−), carboxylate (CH3COO−), fluoride (F−), water, chloride (Cl−), bromide (Br−), iodide (I−), azide (N3−), thiocyanate (SCN−), nitro (NO2−), and nitrate (NO3−). Notably, nitrate is weaker than fluoride as a leaving group. The differences in leaving group stability have direct applications in carboxylic acid derivatives. Compounds with worse leaving groups are more chemically stable, creating a hierarchy of stability that can be exploited in laboratory settings. Amines, which are the worst leaving groups, form the most stable compounds. When a carboxylic acid derivative is attacked by an amine, the product is an amide. Esters are the second most stable, followed by anhydrides, and finally halides, which are the least stable. During an SN2 nucleophilic attack, a partial negative charge develops on the leaving group. In SN1 reactions, the leaving group ionizes and departs completely. Generally, amine, methoxy, and hydroxyl groups do not act as leaving groups in substitution reactions. In non-mechanistic transformations, the leaving group is the actual substituent group present in the substrate and product. The structure of the leaving group significantly affects the rates of both SN1 and SN2 reactions. In general, the more stable the leaving group is as a free species (after it has left), the faster it will leave. This stability is inversely related to the basicity of the species: the more stable the leaving group, the weaker its basicity.
